Risk difference between two groups

Source: R/risk_difference.R
risk_difference.Rd

Reports the absolute risk of a binary outcome in each of two groups and the risk difference between them, with a confidence interval and p-value, as a publication-ready table. The crude analysis uses the Miettinen-Nurminen score method; the adjusted analysis standardises the risks from a logistic regression model. Optionally the number needed to treat (NNTB / NNTH) is added.

Usage

risk_difference(
  data,
  outcome,
  exposure,
  adjust_for = NULL,
  reference = NULL,
  event = NULL,
  event_type = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  format = "gt",
  theme = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

outcome

Binary outcome column. Quoted and bare names are accepted. Logical, numeric 0/1 or 1/2, two-level factor, two-value character and value-labelled (haven) variables are supported.

exposure

Column defining exactly two groups (for example treatment arm or exposure status). Quoted and bare names are accepted.

adjust_for

Optional adjustment variables (quoted or bare names). NULL (default) gives the crude analysis; otherwise the adjusted (standardised) analysis is reported.

reference

Group used as the reference. The risk difference is the other (comparison) group minus the reference group. NULL uses the first factor level, FALSE, 0, or the first value in sorted order.

event

Value of outcome that counts as the event. NULL uses TRUE, 1 (for 0/1 coding), 2 (for 1/2 coding), the second factor level, or the second value in sorted order.

event_type

NULL (default), "harmful" or "beneficial". When given, a column with the number needed to treat is added (see Details). The event direction is needed to tell benefit from harm, so no NNT is shown without it.

conf_level

Confidence level of the interval; default 0.95. It changes the confidence interval only. The p-value is always the two-sided test of a risk difference of zero and does not depend on conf_level, so, for example, a 99% interval can include zero while the p-value is below 0.05.

format

"gt" (default) or "flextable".

theme

Table theme: a preset name ("minimal", "clinical", "striped", "shaded", "jama") or a vector of primitives, as in the regression functions. NULL (default) uses the package default theme ("minimal").

Value

A list of class c("risk_difference", "gtregression") with elements:

table

The rendered gt_tbl or flextable.

table_display

Data frame of the formatted cells as shown.

table_body

Data frame of numeric results, one row per group (reference first): group, events, n, risk, adjusted_risk, adjusted_risk_se, rd, rd_se, rd_low, rd_high, p_value. Risks and differences are proportions. rd_se is the influence-function standard error and is NA for the crude analysis, whose score interval is not based on a single standard error.

footnotes

Character vector of table footnotes.

analysis

"crude" or "adjusted".

outcome, exposure, adjust_for

Variable names.

event, reference, comparison

Resolved event value and groups.

event_type, conf_level

As supplied.

method

List naming the estimate, interval, test and variance methods.

n

List with the numbers of rows supplied, analysed and excluded.

nnt

NULL, or a list with type ("NNTB", "NNTH" or NA), estimate (unrounded, may be Inf), crosses_infinity and segments (data frame with type, from, to; two rows ending at Inf when the interval runs through infinity).

model

The fitted logistic model (adjusted analysis), else NULL. In the model the outcome is .rd_y (1 = event) and the exposure is .rd_a (1 = comparison group).

variable_labels, level_labels, theme

Labels and theme used for display.

source, format

"risk_difference"; "gt" or "flextable".

Details

Absolute risk and risk difference. The risk in a group is the proportion of its members with the event. The risk difference (RD) is the risk in the comparison group minus the risk in the reference group. It is stored as a difference of proportions (for example -0.08) and shown in percentage points (-8.0). A negative RD means that the event is less frequent in the comparison group. For a harmful event (for example death) a negative RD is an absolute risk reduction and a positive RD an absolute risk increase; for a beneficial event (for example cure) the reading is reversed. These are readings of the same number, not separate estimates, and the table reports the signed RD only. The resolved event, reference and comparison are stored in the result, are always written in the table footnote, and are announced in a message whenever they were inferred from anything other than logical or 0/1 coding.

Analysis population. One complete-case population is used: observations with a missing outcome or exposure (and, for the adjusted analysis, any missing adjustment variable) are excluded. The numbers supplied, analysed and excluded are stored and the footnote reports them.

Crude analysis (adjust_for = NULL). Risks are the observed proportions. The confidence interval is the Miettinen-Nurminen score interval (restricted maximum-likelihood variance with the \(N/(N-1)\) factor, no continuity correction) and the p-value comes from the same score statistic at a difference of zero (equal to Pearson's chi-square multiplied by \((N-1)/N\)). The method is defined when a group has no events or only events; when no one, or everyone, has the event the p-value is 1.

Adjusted analysis. A main-effects logistic regression of the outcome on the exposure and the adjustment variables is fitted. Each person's risk is predicted twice from their own covariates, once as a member of each group; the predictions are averaged over the analysis population to give the two adjusted (standardised) risks, and their difference is the adjusted RD. The table shows the observed events and group sizes next to the adjusted risks. The standard error is the influence-function standard error of the stacked estimating equations (logistic score equations and the two averages), which accounts for the estimation of the model and for the sampling of the covariates and does not rely on the logistic model being correct. The confidence interval is a Wald interval, with limits restricted to the range -1 to 1, and the p-value is two-sided normal. No small-sample correction is applied; in simulations with about 80 to 100 participants coverage of the 95% interval was about 94%. The analysis stops with an error, and returns no table, when the model does not converge, when fitted probabilities reach 0 or 1 (separation, including a group with no events or only events), when the exposure or an adjustment variable is aliased, or when the outcome is constant.

Interpretation. The function describes a calculation and makes no causal claim. In an individually randomised trial the adjusted RD is a covariate-adjusted estimate of the marginal treatment difference, and it remains valid when the logistic model is not exactly right (see the FDA 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment). In a non-randomised study it is a standardised risk difference; it can be read causally only if there is no unmeasured confounding, the outcome model is correct and the groups overlap in their covariates.

NNTB and NNTH. With event_type, the number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute value of the unrounded RD, shown rounded up to a whole person. It is labelled NNTB (number needed to treat for one additional person to benefit) when the comparison group does better and NNTH (for one additional person to be harmed) when it does worse: for a harmful event a negative RD gives NNTB and a positive RD NNTH, and the reverse for a beneficial event. When the confidence interval of the RD includes zero, the interval of the NNT runs from a finite NNTB through infinity to a finite NNTH and is shown and stored in that form (Altman 1998), never as a pair of finite limits. The NNT applies to the follow-up period of the study and assumes that the RD reflects what the intervention does.

Limits of this version. Binary outcome at a fixed follow-up; exactly two groups; independent observations; main-effects logistic model for adjustment. Not supported: more than two groups, continuous exposures, stratified (Mantel-Haenszel) or clustered designs, non-inferiority margins, time-to-event outcomes. The result can be printed, saved with save_table and relabelled with modify_table (caption, caveat, labels and headers only); it is not accepted by merge_tables or the forest-plot functions.

References

Miettinen O, Nurminen M (1985). Comparative analysis of two rates. Statistics in Medicine, 4(2), 213-226.

Newcombe RG (1998). Interval estimation for the difference between independent proportions: comparison of eleven methods. Statistics in Medicine, 17(8), 873-890.

Altman DG (1998). Confidence intervals for the number needed to treat. BMJ, 317(7168), 1309-1312.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2023). Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products: Guidance for Industry.

See also

uni_reg and multi_reg for relative measures (odds ratios, risk ratios).

Examples

# Crude: low birth weight by maternal smoking
rd <- risk_difference(data_birthwt, low, smoke)
rd$table_display
#>   Group Events / N  Risk Risk difference (95% CI) p-value
#> 1     0   29 / 115 25.2%                     Ref.        
#> 2     1    30 / 74 40.5%       15.3 (1.7 to 29.0)   0.027
rd$footnotes
#> [1] "Risk = proportion with the event (low = 1). Risk difference = 1 − 0 (groups of smoke), in percentage points."
#> [2] "Confidence interval and p-value: Miettinen–Nurminen score method."                                           
#> [3] "N = 189; no observations excluded."                                                                          
#> [4] "CI = confidence interval; Ref. = reference group."                                                           

# Adjusted (standardised), with the number needed to treat
adj <- risk_difference(
  data_birthwt, "low", "smoke",
  adjust_for = c("age", "lwt"),
  event_type = "harmful",
  format = "flextable"
)
adj$table_display
#>   Group Events / N Adjusted risk Adjusted risk difference (95% CI) p-value
#> 1     0   29 / 115         25.7%                              Ref.        
#> 2     1    30 / 74         39.7%                14.1 (0.3 to 27.8)   0.045
#>        NNT (95% CI)
#> 1                  
#> 2 NNTH 8 (4 to 303)
adj$table_body
#>   group events   n      risk adjusted_risk adjusted_risk_se        rd
#> 1     0     29 115 0.2521739     0.2565853       0.04063451        NA
#> 2     1     30  74 0.4054054     0.3972194       0.05724837 0.1406341
#>        rd_se      rd_low   rd_high    p_value
#> 1         NA          NA        NA         NA
#> 2 0.07006438 0.003310438 0.2779578 0.04472704
adj$nnt
#> $type
#> [1] "NNTH"
#> 
#> $estimate
#> [1] 7.110651
#> 
#> $crosses_infinity
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $segments
#>   type     from       to
#> 1 NNTH 3.597669 302.0748
#> 

# Factor coding: name the event and the reference explicitly
bw <- data_birthwt
bw$smoking <- factor(bw$smoke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
bw$weight <- factor(bw$low, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Normal", "Low"))
risk_difference(bw, weight, smoking, event = "Low", reference = "No",
                conf_level = 0.90)$table_display
#>   Group Events / N  Risk Risk difference (90% CI) p-value
#> 1    No   29 / 115 25.2%                     Ref.        
#> 2   Yes    30 / 74 40.5%       15.3 (3.9 to 26.8)   0.027
